Inspired by the positive response on my first post and because I'm on vacation and don't know how to relax with a good book like my wife, and also because I enjoy practicing my English and provide Voat with content, here comes another keto rant!

Note: If you are a native English speaker and enjoy this read you can help me out by pointing out and explain some grammar mistakes. I really appreciate it.

About me: I'm and IT-guy/generalist. My passion is to look into problems with systems and processes, find and understand the information needed to solve them. Do that. Feel good about it and move on. I've used the same approach when fixing my own medical issues. Before I trusted doctors and general health advice until I stumbled over keto and the alternative information surrounding it. These days I trust doctors no more than I trust my own parents (which both are doctors by the way). No references will be given to back up my trail of thoughts, but please point out if you think things don't add up and why. I've been studying this on and off for about four years. I've read Taubes, Lustig, Yudkin, Price and many others. I don't claim to be right about anything. These are hypotheses and they have changed over time and will continue to do so.

What are processed foods?

Processed foods are foods that's been made in some kind of industrial process. It's hard to draw a line, and some foods that can be considered processed by this broad definition are probably not that unhealthy. And some foods that does not fall under this definition are in fact quite unhealthy. I still think this is a good and simple enough guideline that lets you avoid most bad food. Another way to put it is - Don't eat what your grandmother would not recognize as food.

Why are processed foods bad?

The main reason are the favorite ingredients food manufacturers like to put into them for different reasons. More on this below.

Sugar - Sugar is of course on the top of the list. Pure sugar is rarely found in nature and was an expensive commodity before the industrial age. Today sugar is a blessing for food producers and are an ingredient in almost all products. It's cheap and it is a both sweetener and a conservative. Almost anything can be made palatable and given a long shelf life by adding sugar.

The problem with sugar however is that it is toxic to us in high doses and the body must therefor quickly convert it into glycogen and move it to the energy stores in our muscles. Our body uses the hormone insulin for this and if we eat moderate amounts of sugar all is fine. But if we ingest too much we can get into trouble because our energy stores are limited. When the muscle stores are full, the body must find other ways to get rid of the sugar. It then tells the liver to start converting the sugar to fat and our fat tissue gets primed to bring in fat from the bloodstream, thus limiting the triglycerides (fats) in the blood which also needs to be kept in check just like sugar. Our metabolism is also switched over to "sugar burning mode". If we over consume sugar under prolonged periods the next process begins - we get fat. And as you can see from the process above this makes perfect sense. The body simply needs bigger energy stores since it constantly needs to evacuate sugar from the blood stream to keep us alive.

Processed vegetable oils - This is a biggie. The food industry has unchecked been able to use the world as a test lab for different kinds of cheap vegetable fats for over a century. In the early 1900 Crisco and other types of processed vegetable fats was introduced to the market. A huge financial success because they where made of stuff that before could only be used for things like paint or candles. It was cheap to make and didn't turn rancid like butter. Several decades later it was discovered however that these kinds of fat most likely was the main cause of the heart attack epidemic in the 50s and 60s. When vegetable fats are hardened in a chemical process some of the fat molecules transform into something that is very harmful - trans fats. In later years, the amount of trans fats in processed vegetable oils are much lower because of more advanced refining processes, but they are still unhealthy. The food industry tries to associate processed vegetable oils with healthy natural fats like fish or (virgin) olive oil, calling them unsaturated. The unsaturated aspect of fat has however very little to do with how healthy they are. Truth is that most processed vegetable oils are harmful which have been confirmed in trials.

But the food industry love these fats for about the same reason they love using sugar - It's cheap, makes food tasty and it acts as a conservative. Cookies made of real butter gets old after a few weeks. Not so when made with margarine. The creepy part with this is that the reason we dislike rancid natural fats is because they have oxidized and are unhealthy for us. Processed vegetable oils have the same type of fat molecules as oxidized natural fat. Hence we are eating a type of fat that should make us throw up because of it's harmfulness. Food for thought don't you think? (pun intended).

Starch and refined grains - the hidden sugars. Starch and especially wheat have the same capacity to raise blood sugar to harmful levels as sugar. In fact white bread has a higher glycemic index than table sugar, meaning is raises the blood sugar quicker. But starch and refined grains also have other problems associated with it. Starch sticks to the teeth and promote the type of bacteria that causes cavities. It's been shown that Egyptian mummies had bad dental health and it's believed they had a diet consisting of much grain but very limited access to sugar.

Starch and grains also seems to cause problems with our intestinal bacteria and immune system. The reasons are unclear, but I think it's reasonable to speculate that they promote the same kind of bacteria as in the mouth. Many products also have flower in them which have not been raised properly. The fermentation process is accelerated when making industrial bread for time saving reasons. But the rising is important because it breaks down so called anti nutrients. And as you know starch and refined grains is another main ingredient of processed foods, because it's cheap and gives nice taste and texture.

Soy products - This is a quite new and suspicious ingredient in modern processed foods. It contains hormone like proteins and the effects on humans are unclear. In Asia, soy has never been used as a staple food product. It has always been fermented in some way before eating, and consumed in small amounts. For example as sauce. I prefer to stay clear. But the food industry promotes this as a healthy alternative to the "oh so unhealthy" dairy products...

Combining and chemistry - The main reason processed foods are bad is because of the ingredients, but another problem is how these ingredients are combined to make processed foods as palatable and addictive as possible. Processed food producers are like drug designers, and have a scientific approach when combining these cheap ingredients to something that is irresistible and promotes overeating. The same goes for pet food by the way. Cats and dogs are even less tolerable to sugar, starch and processed vegetable oils and attracts diabetes and cancer because of the bad quality pet food we give them.

I hope this lays it out for you why it's preferable to stay clear of processed foods. But remember all is not black and white. You can get away with some bad food on occasion. It's the dosage that makes the poison.

First, you write really well for someone who is not a native speaker. I am on my phone. So, it is hard for me to go through everything in detail. But, here are a couple quick things I saw.

If you are a native English speaker and enjoy this read you can help me out by pointing out and explain some grammar mistakes.

s/explain/explaining ... All your verbs should be in the same tense. You ask us to help by pointing so we should also be explaining.

Before I trusted doctors and general health advice until I stumbled over keto and the alternative information surrounding it.

Ah, this is one of those difficult to explain English rules. When you start a sentence with "Before" you actually talk about the second thing first. For example:

Before I stumbled over keto and the alternative information surrounding it, I trusted doctors and general health advice.

This could also be written:

I trusted doctors and general health advice before I stumbled over keto and the alternative information surrounding it.

Or

I trusted doctors and general health advice until I stumbled over keto and the alternative information surrounding it.

Generally, you won't use before and until in the same sentence. It is possible to use them together, but you will typically end up confusing people even when you do it correctly.

Another way to think about it is that the thing that comes first goes before the "before" in a sentence. If you can't put it before the before (because you started the sentence with before) use a comma after the second event and put the first event after the comma.

I hope that isn't hopelessly confusing. These things often make sense to English speakers because we are exposed to them from a young age.
